explanations.explanation: John the Baptist keeps it short: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.” (Matthew 3:2) That's the whole sermon. To repent is to turn around, and he wants the people to do it because the kingdom is close. I've seen cookie recipes with more words than that.

Rejoice is a lovely word, friend, and I'd gladly press it into a cookie. It just isn't what John says. He says, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.” The kingdom being near is the news, and repent is what he tells them to do about it.

Gather makes sense, since a lot of people do show up to John in the wilderness (Matthew 3:5). But gathering isn't what he tells them to do. He says, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.” The crowd comes, and the word he preaches to them is repent.

The voice in the wilderness calls, “Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.” Matthew says that voice is John, and he's talking about the prophet Isaiah's words. So John isn't clearing a road for himself. He's getting people ready for the Lord.

A king sounds like the kind of person you'd roll out a road for. But Isaiah's words never mention one. The voice says, “Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.” The way is for the Lord.

Priests are a fair guess, since they're tied to the temple. But the text doesn't point there. Isaiah's voice says, “Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.” That road is for the Lord, friend, and nobody else gets named.
True. Matthew says, “His food was locusts and wild honey.” That's the whole menu out there. I've served some strange cookie batches in my day, but I have never once put locusts on the tray.
It's actually true, friend. Matthew says, “His food was locusts and wild honey.” Locusts are insects, and the honey is wild. So John's wilderness menu is real, and it's short.

explanations.answer: People from Jerusalem and all Judea and around the Jordan
explanations.explanation: That's it. Matthew says, “People went out to him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan.” Jerusalem was the big city, and they still walked out to the wilderness. I've had folks skip my bakery over a little rain, so this is impressive.

explanations.answer: A few shepherds from the hills around Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Matthew never names any shepherds or Bethlehem here. And it's no "few," friend. The text says people went out to John “from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan.” That's a much bigger crowd.

explanations.answer: A few traders passing through on the road from Tyre
explanations.explanation: Traders are a fun picture, but they aren't in this verse. Matthew says, “People went out to him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan.” That's way more than a few travelers. Think crowds from the whole area.
True. Matthew says, “Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.” They aren't just getting wet. They're owning up out loud, in front of everybody. That takes real nerve.

It's actually true. Matthew 3:6 says, “Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.” The baptizing and the confessing happen together. Owning up in public isn't easy, so I'm proud of every one of them.

That's what he says. John sees the Pharisees and Sadducees coming and calls out, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” There's no warm-up. I greet my customers with a smile, and he opened with a snake.

John isn't butttering anybody up here. He sees the Pharisees and Sadducees, religious leaders, and says, “You brood of vipers…” No title, no bow. Honored teachers is a much nicer greeting, but it isn't the one in the text.

Faithful shepherds would be a warm hello, friend, but John doesn't say it. The text says, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” Those are his first words to the Pharisees and Sadducees. Quite a different tone.

Fruit is the word. John says, “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance.” He's saying real repentance shows up in what a person does. A cookie box that's empty isn't a box, friend, and the same goes here.

Offerings sound religious enough to fit, but they aren't John's word. He says, “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance.” Fruit is something you can see growing. That's what he wants to see with their repentance.

Prayers are good, and Scripture speaks well of them, but they aren't the word here. John says, “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance.” He's asking for something that shows. Fruit is what he calls for.

It's the other way around, friend. John says, “And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’” Abraham, Israel's forefather, matters, but John won't let them lean on his name. Having him as a father isn't enough on its own.

False is right. John tells them, “And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’” He's not letting them hide behind Abraham, Israel's forefather. It's like claiming you can bake because your grandma's famous cookies exist.

Stones, friend. John says, “For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.” He's probably pointing at the ground around them, and I think that landed hard. If God can do that with rocks, nobody gets to lean on their family name.
Waters feels natural, since John's standing at the Jordan. But the text says something else. John says, “out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.” Stones, not waters.

Reeds grow by a river, so I see why you'd pick them. John doesn't mention them, though. He says, “For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.” A stone is a lot harder than a reed, which makes the point stronger.

explanations.answer: It is cut down and thrown into the fire
explanations.explanation: That's his picture. John says, “The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” He means it, too. Notice it says every tree, with no exceptions.

explanations.answer: It is dug around and given another year
explanations.explanation: A second chance is a kind picture, but it isn't what John says here. He says every tree that “does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” The axe is already at the root. His message in this moment is urgent.

explanations.answer: It is left standing alone in the field
explanations.explanation: John doesn't leave any tree standing there. He says, “The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” Cut down and thrown into the fire. That's the whole picture.

It's the opposite, friend. John says, “after me will come One more powerful than I.” He's the one doing the baptizing, and he still says Someone greater is coming. That's a humble thing for a preacher to say.

False is right. John says, “after me will come One more powerful than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.” Even with a whole crowd coming out to him, he says the One after him is greater. That's humble, and I'm taking notes.

Sandals, yes. John says the One coming is “One more powerful than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.” That's about as low a job as he can think of, and he says he isn't even worthy of it. Picture the most important person you know and think how small that job feels.
Pouring water on hands sounds like something a servant would do. But John doesn't say it. He says the One coming has “sandals I am not worthy to carry.” His job, he says, is the sandals.

Holding a cloak is a fair guess for a humble job, but it's not in the text. John says of the One coming, “whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.” The sandals are what he names. And he says he isn't worthy of even that.

That's what John says. “I baptize you with water for repentance, but after me will come One more powerful than I… He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” Water is what John has, and the One coming has something greater. John says so himself.
Oil and incense feel holy, but John doesn't say them. He says the One coming “will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” John uses water. The One after him uses the Holy Spirit and fire.

The cloud and the sea show up in Paul's letter to the Corinthians about Israel's journey (1 Corinthians 10:1-2). But that's not what John is saying here. He says the One coming “will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” This is a different sentence entirely.

Chaff is it. John says, “His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather His wheat into the barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.” Wheat goes in the barn. The chaff burns with unquenchable fire.
Thorns would burn nicely, but John doesn't use them in this picture. He's on a threshing floor, where the wheat goes into the barn. He says, “He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

Branches belong to the tree picture a few verses back (Matthew 3:10), friend. This picture is about harvest. John says the wheat gets gathered into the barn, “but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”
Baptized, yes. Matthew says, “Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John.” He travels all that way for it. Jesus is the One John was just talking about, so this is a big moment.
Taught is a reasonable thing to expect at a gathering like this. But Matthew tells us why Jesus came. He “came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John.” Baptism is the reason for the trip.
Blessed feels right, but it isn't the word. Matthew says Jesus “came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John.” He came to be baptized.

explanations.answer: I need to be baptized by You
explanations.explanation: That's his answer. John says, “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” I think he's stunned, and honestly, I would be too. A man who just said he isn't worthy to carry the sandals now has this One standing in front of him.
Matthew doesn't mention any disciples of John here, and John doesn't hand the job off. He says, “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” He's speaking for himself.

explanations.answer: You must go back to Galilee
explanations.explanation: John doesn't send Jesus home. He tries to prevent Him, saying, “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” It's a question full of surprise. Galilee never comes up in his words.

True. Jesus says, “Let it be so now. It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way.” Then Matthew says, “Then John permitted Him.” John was hesitating a moment earlier, and now he goes ahead.
John does go ahead, friend. First he tries to prevent Jesus. Then Jesus answers, “Let it be so now,” and Matthew says, “Then John permitted Him.” So John says yes after hearing Jesus.

Right. Matthew says Jesus “saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him.” John had just said the One coming would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. Now the Spirit of God rests on Jesus Himself.
Angels do show up a lot in Scripture, but not here. Matthew says Jesus “saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him.” That's the One who comes down.
Elijah was a prophet in Israel's past, and he's not in this scene. Matthew says Jesus “saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him.” The Spirit of God is who Jesus sees.

explanations.answer: This is My beloved Son in whom I am well pleased
explanations.explanation: That's the voice. “And a voice from heaven said, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!’” God Himself speaks. And He says it right after Jesus comes up out of the water.

explanations.answer: This is My chosen servant who will rule the nations
explanations.explanation: That sounds close, but those aren't the words. The voice from heaven says, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!” The voice calls Jesus Son, and says He is well pleased.

explanations.answer: This is the prophet who will lead My people home
explanations.explanation: Prophet isn't the word the voice uses. It says, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!” The voice names Jesus as Son. That's the heart of what's said.
